# Language Models from the Ground Up

By Rolling Edition, with AI · **Foundations** · [Read it free online](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up)

[![The latest edition's stamp](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/stamp.svg)](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up) [![Checks](https://github.com/rollingedition/book-language-models-from-the-ground-up/actions/workflows/checks.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/rollingedition/book-language-models-from-the-ground-up/actions/workflows/checks.yml)

How a language model works, built one part at a time: next-word prediction, tokens, embeddings, a neural model, attention and the transformer, training a small model on a CPU, choosing words, what an open model holds inside, and how instruction tuning changes it.

**Written with AI. Verified by people.** [How we make books](https://rollingedition.com/policies/editorial) · [Check a copy](https://rollingedition.com/check)

## Who it's for

For readers comfortable with Python and NumPy who are new to how language models work: a developer who calls LLM APIs and wants to know what happens inside, or a data scientist moving into language work.

| | Chapter | By the end, you can | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Predicting the next word](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/predicting-the-next-word) · [source](chapters/01-predicting-the-next-word.md) | build a complete language model from counts, use it to suggest the next word as a shopper types, generate text with it, and measure with one number how well it predicts text it has never seen | 8 |
| 2 | [Tokens](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/tokens) · [source](chapters/02-tokens.md) | build a byte-pair encoding tokenizer from scratch, choose its vocabulary size by measuring what each size costs, and read the tokenizer of an open language model well enough to apply its merges by hand | 7 |
| 3 | [Counting further back](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/counting-further-back) · [source](chapters/03-counting-further-back.md) | build an n-gram language model that looks several tokens back, smooth it with Kneser-Ney so it handles text it hasn't seen (smoothing gives some probability to what the counts never saw, as chapter 1 showed), and measure the baseline that every neural model in this book is measured against | 7 |
| 4 | [Words as vectors](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/words-as-vectors) · [source](chapters/04-words-as-vectors.md) | turn every token of the store's text into a short vector of numbers, so that tokens used in similar ways get similar vectors, by two methods: compressing counts of which tokens appear together, and training a small model to predict each token's neighbours | 8 |
| 5 | [A neural language model](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/a-neural-language-model) · [source](chapters/05-a-neural-language-model.md) | build a neural language model that predicts the next token from a window of earlier tokens, compute its gradients by hand and check them, train it with PyTorch, and measure it fairly against the counted baseline | 10 |
| 6 | [Attention](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/attention) · [source](chapters/06-attention.md) | compute attention by hand: score how well each token's query matches every earlier token's key, turn the scores into weights, and average the values those weights select | 8 |
| 7 | [The transformer block](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/the-transformer-block) · [source](chapters/07-the-transformer-block.md) | assemble a transformer block from its parts, joined by residual connections: attention, normalization, a gated feed-forward layer and position information | 8 |
| 8 | [Training a small model](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/training-a-small-model) · [source](chapters/08-training-a-small-model.md) | train a small transformer from start to finish and judge the result | 7 |
| 9 | [Choosing the next token](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/choosing-the-next-token) · [source](chapters/09-choosing-the-next-token.md) | turn a language model's probabilities into text, and choose how: always the likeliest token, the likeliest whole text by beam search, or a sample shaped by a temperature, a top-k or top-p cut, a repetition penalty and a minimum length | 7 |
| 10 | [Inside an open model](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/inside-an-open-model) · [source](chapters/10-inside-an-open-model.md) | read an open language model with what this book has built: count where its parameters go, work out what it costs to run, score text with it fairly against a model with a different tokenizer, find the attention patterns of chapter 6 in its heads, and test what it copies | 7 |
| 11 | [From predicting to following instructions](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/from-predicting-to-following) · [source](chapters/11-from-predicting-to-following.md) | explain how a model that predicts the next token becomes one that follows requests, build the two training losses that do it, and measure what that change does and doesn't fix | 9 |

## Run the examples

Every example runs offline, in a pinned environment, and its output must match the book's. With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

```sh
uv venv --python 3.12.15
uv pip install -r examples/requirements.txt
cd examples && ../.venv/bin/python store-text.py
```

Model outputs are recorded once in `examples/data/recorded/`, each folder with a `manifest.json` that names the model, its exact version and the script that recorded it, so the examples never call a model. `recordings/` holds the scripts that record them again.

Where the data comes from, and its licence: [`examples/data/smollm2-tokenizer/README.md`](examples/data/smollm2-tokenizer/README.md), [`examples/data/wands-text/README.md`](examples/data/wands-text/README.md).

## How this book stays current

When a library this book uses releases a new version, every example runs again in the new version. Agents draft any fix and check every change, and a change merges once its checks pass; one with a serious risk, such as a security or copyright problem, waits for a Rolling Edition maintainer. Anyone can check the book or correct it with a pull request. Each new edition is stamped with its date, its examples passing and what changed. [See what changed in each edition](https://rollingedition.com/language-models-from-the-ground-up/changes).
